FOR INDEPENDENT ICE DAM REMOVAL CONTRACTORS

A rate that works on a long run can lose money on a short one.

A crew, a truck, and a steam machine cost nearly the same to dispatch whether the eave that needs clearing is 15 feet or 150 feet — so a flat per-foot rate card that comfortably covers a long roof can fall short of a short job's largely fixed cost. This free calculator prices a job from footage, crew, and an emergency premium, checks whether your rate card actually clears this job's break-even rate, and lets you plug in the real on-site hours once the ice is off.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser. Your job details, prices, and hours are never uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is saved when you close the tab. "Copy share link" encodes your footage, rates, and crew figures into this page's own URL — nothing is sent to a server, and the link is only ever built and copied in your browser. We count only anonymous local feature events (quote-priced, actual-hours-checked, share_link_copied) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no job details, prices, or hours are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Why can a per-linear-foot rate card lose money on a short job?

Because sending a crew, a truck, and a steam machine costs close to the same whether the eave that needs clearing is 15 feet or 150 feet. A rate that clears its cost comfortably on a long run gets spread across far fewer feet on a short one, so the same rate can fall short of the job's real, largely fixed cost.

What does breakEvenRatePerFoot actually tell me?

It is the per-foot rate this specific job's footage would need, ignoring your minimum service charge, to just cover its real cost with no profit. If your rate card is below that number, only your minimum service charge is protecting you on a job this short — and if the minimum itself is set too low, the job is a real loss.

Why is the emergency premium applied to labor and travel but not to fuel or equipment?

Because the premium compensates for being available outside normal hours, not for extra difficulty or extra fuel use — the steam machine burns the same fuel at 2am as at 2pm. It only changes what billed crew time costs.

Does anything about my job details or prices get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-linear-foot.html.text:
← Ice Dam Removal Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-foot rate card

$7/ft × 80 feet is $560 whether the dispatch is a scheduled Tuesday afternoon or a midnight call during a storm, and whether the crew is back down the ladder in 2.5 hours or 4.5. A rate card cannot see either difference; this calculator prices both.

What a flat per-foot rate card is

A per-foot rate card is the fastest way to quote over the phone: multiply the footage a customer describes by a number and read off a price. It is easy to compare between competing bids, and it is the number a prospect holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number was set once, for an ordinary scheduled job, and then reused for every call afterward — including the ones that are not ordinary: a storm-night dispatch with an after-hours premium, or a job where the ice turns out thicker than the phone estimate assumed.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the footage, crew size and hourly pay, travel hours and miles, steamer fuel and equipment cost, whether the call is an emergency dispatch, overhead, target margin, and a minimum service charge. It turns the actual cost into a price, a break-even rate per foot for that footage, and — once the crew is back down the ladder — a check of the real profit against the actual on-site hours, not the estimate the quote was built on.

What a flat per-foot rate card doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $560 for an 80-foot job whether it is a scheduled daytime call or a storm-night emergency dispatch — a labor and travel premium the per-foot number never sees. Applies the entered emergency premium to labor and travel time only, never to fuel or equipment, so a storm call's real cost is priced in before the quote goes out.
On the calculator's own default 80-foot job, the $560 rate-card quote leaves about $227.98 profit (a 40.71% margin) on a scheduled call. Reports that the identical job dispatched as an emergency costs about $425.32 to run — the same $560 quote now leaves about $134.68, a 24.05% margin, about $47.60 short of the price that would hold the 30% target margin.
Locks in a price from the phone-estimate footage and hours, with no way to check it once the crew has actually been on the roof. Recomputes cost from the actual on-site hours once the job is done: the same job estimated at 2.5 hours per tech but running 4.5 (thicker ice than expected) drops profit from about $227.98 to about $75.66 without the quoted price ever changing.
Bakes overhead into a round per-foot number nobody re-derives. Loads the entered overhead percentage onto direct cost every time, so overhead tracks the actual job rather than a memorized rate.
Gives a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the break-even rate per foot and the real profit and margin, so a rate card can be scored against real cost instead of assumed to be fine.

A flat per-foot rate card is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when a call turns out to be an emergency dispatch or the hours run past the estimate, and nothing about a per-foot number tells you when either has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Does a flat per-foot rate card charge more for an emergency call?

Not unless the operator remembers to mark it up by hand. A rate card is just feet times a number, so an 80-foot job prices at the same $560 whether it is a scheduled Tuesday afternoon appointment or a midnight dispatch during a storm. This calculator applies the entered emergency premium to labor and travel time -- never to fuel or equipment, which cost the same at 2am as at 2pm -- so the real cost of a storm call shows up before the quote goes out.

How much does an unpriced emergency call actually cost in margin?

On this calculator's own default 80-foot job -- a two-person crew at $34/hr each, 2.5 estimated on-site hours, 1 hour of travel, 35 round-trip miles, $20 of steamer fuel, $15 of equipment cost, 12% overhead, a 30% target margin, and a 35% emergency premium -- a scheduled call costs about $332.02 to run and the $560 rate-card quote leaves roughly $227.98 profit, a 40.71% margin. The identical job dispatched as a storm-night emergency costs about $425.32 to run once the premium hits labor and travel; the same $560 quote now leaves about $134.68, a 24.05% margin -- about $47.60 short of the price that would actually hold the 30% target margin.

Does a rate card check itself against the hours the crew actually worked?

No -- a rate card is set from the phone-estimate footage before the truck rolls and never revisited. This calculator does: on the same default job, if the ice turns out thicker than the phone estimate and the crew's 2.5 estimated on-site hours become 4.5 actual hours, the $560 quote does not change but the real cost rises to about $484.34, cutting profit from about $227.98 down to about $75.66 without the operator ever being told the margin moved.

Is a flat per-foot rate card ever the right way to quote?

For a run of similar, scheduled, daytime jobs with dependable ice thickness, a flat rate card can land close enough. The risk is the two things it cannot see by itself: whether a specific call is an emergency dispatch, and whether the hours actually spent match what the phone estimate assumed. Neither shows up in a per-foot number until the invoice is already written.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the footage, crew, travel, fuel, equipment cost, emergency premium, overhead, and target margin you enter, plus the actual on-site hours once the job is done, and turns that into a price, a break-even rate per foot, and a real profit and margin -- the arithmetic a flat rate card skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-foot rate card is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until a call turns out to be an emergency dispatch or the hours run past the estimate. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $332.02, $560.00, $227.98, $425.32, $134.68, $47.60, $484.34, and $75.66 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on its own default example job, not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs.

Open the Ice Dam Removal Bid Calculator to price your own job, or see why a flat rate card can lose money on a short job and this calculator vs. Jobber.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a roofing or ice-condition assessment. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, fuel, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free and experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use it as a system of record.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a service company's whole operation, including scheduling a storm-response dispatch and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this ice dam removal job cost, given its footage, crew, and minimum service charge, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home and trade service businesses — lawn care, cleaning, HVAC, roofing and gutter, and other seasonal or storm-response trades among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew or driver dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling a job, dispatching a crew, and invoicing and collecting payment once a price already exists; none describe working out whether a short job's per-foot rate card actually covers a two-person crew's largely fixed dispatch cost, or reconciling a job's price against the actual on-site hours once the ice turns out thicker than the phone estimate assumed — which is what this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a customer list, schedule a crew's storm-response route, or collect a payment. It takes linear feet of roof edge, crew size and hourly pay, travel hours and miles, steamer fuel and equipment cost, an emergency/storm-dispatch premium, overhead and target margin, and a minimum service charge, and turns that into the price to quote, the break-even rate per foot for this job's specific footage, and the profit if the job goes as estimated — plus, once the crew is back down the ladder, a check of the actual on-site hours against that same breakeven, so a per-foot rate that only survives on a short job because of the minimum charge shows up clearly, instead of as a surprise on the invoice. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most ice dam removal contractors get different value from each: Jobber (or a comparable field service platform) for managing customers, scheduling crews and collecting payment across an ongoing business as an account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one job should cost from its footage and crew before it is quoted, and whether a real on-site hour count still clears the breakeven once the job is done. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled dispatch, an invoice, or a signed work order.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Jobber?

They do different jobs, and an ice dam removal contractor of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Jobber is a field service management platform used across home and trade service businesses — including seasonal and storm-response trades — to run client management and quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. This calculator does one narrower thing: it takes a job's linear feet of roof edge, crew size and pay, travel, steamer fuel and equipment cost, an emergency-dispatch premium, and a minimum service charge, and turns that into the price to quote, the break-even rate per foot for that specific footage, and — once the crew is back down the ladder — the real profit and margin the job actually left. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A contractor already scheduling storm-response dispatch, invoicing customers, and taking payments across a crew or a fleet of trucks is better served by Jobber or a comparable field service platform; a contractor who wants an instant, private answer to what one job should cost before it is quoted, and whether a short job's rate card actually clears its own fixed cost, is in the right place here.

why-a-flat-rate-card-can-lose-money-on-a.text:
← Ice dam removal bid calculator

Why a flat rate card can lose money on a short job

A per-linear-foot rate card looks like it prices every job fairly: more feet, more money. But the crew, the truck, and the steam machine cost close to the same to send out whether the eave needing ice cleared is 15 feet or 150 feet — the trip's real cost is mostly fixed, not proportional to the number quoted. A rate that comfortably clears cost on a long roof can leave a short job depending entirely on the minimum service charge, and if that minimum was never actually checked against real cost, the short job is a loss.

Open the free ice dam removal calculator

Why this is easy to get wrong

The long jobs hide it. An 80-foot job at $7/ft — a typical single-family eave — prices out to $560, comfortably above the roughly $332 it actually costs to dispatch a two-person crew, drive out, and run the steamer. Everything looks healthy, because on a job this size the fixed trip cost is a small share of the total.

Minimum service charges often get set once and never checked. A round number like $200 or $250 sounds like a safe floor for "a small job," until you actually add up a two-person crew's labor, travel, fuel, and equipment cost and find it comes to more than that minimum before a single foot is billed.

The risk shows up exactly on the calls that feel easiest to say yes to. A short spot over one window sounds like a quick, low-effort job — but it still needs the same truck roll and the same two-person crew as a full-house job, so it is the shortest jobs, not the longest ones, where an unchecked minimum charge actually loses money.

Worked example

The default job above — an 80-foot eave, a two-person crew at $34/hr each, 2.5 estimated on-site hours, 1 hour of travel, 35 round-trip miles, $20 of steamer fuel, $15 of equipment cost, 12% overhead — costs about $332.02 to run. At the $7/ft rate card, that same crew and truck sent to a 15-foot job (one bad spot over a window) only bills $105.00 from the rate card alone — the minimum service charge is the only thing standing between that job and a loss:

FigureMinimum set at $375Minimum set at $200
Rate-card price (15ft × $7/ft)$105.00$105.00
Minimum service charge$375.00$200.00
Quoted price (the higher of the two)$375.00$200.00
Real job cost (crew, travel, fuel, equipment, overhead)$332.02$332.02
Break-even rate this footage needs (ignoring the minimum)$22.13/ft$22.13/ft
Profit$42.98−$132.02

The $7/ft rate card is nowhere near the $22.13/ft this specific 15-foot job would need to break even on its own — in both columns, only the minimum service charge is doing the work. A $375 minimum still clears the job's real cost with a thin profit; a $200 minimum, which might look perfectly reasonable next to a competitor's advertised "starting at $199," does not even cover the crew and truck that showed up. The calculator's underpriced flag catches exactly this case, and breakEvenRatePerFoot tells you the number to check your minimum against for any footage, not just this example.

Common questions

How do I know if my ice dam removal rate card is priced correctly for a short job?

Compare your per-foot rate to the break-even rate for this job's specific footage, not to what feels reasonable for a typical job. A crew, truck, and steam machine cost close to the same to send out regardless of footage, so a short job's break-even rate per foot is much higher than a long job's.

Why would a job with a minimum service charge still lose money?

Because the minimum charge is only a backstop if it is actually set above the job's real fixed cost. A minimum that was set by guessing, or copied from a competitor's rate card, can sit below what a two-person crew, a truck, and a steam machine really cost to dispatch once labor, travel, fuel, and overhead are added up.

Does raising the per-foot rate fix the short-job problem?

Only up to a point, and it makes long jobs more expensive than they need to be. Raising the minimum service charge to actually clear the job's fixed cost protects short calls without touching the price of a long run, where the per-foot rate was already working fine.

How do I know if a specific job is at risk before I quote it?

Short footage on a job that still needs a full crew dispatch is the signal — a single ice dam over one window or a short run of eave, rather than a whole house. The calculator's break-even-rate-per-foot figure recomputes for the exact footage you enter, so you can check any specific job before quoting it rather than relying on a rule of thumb.
